cover_design.ringkas: A self-study course in Javanese for complete beginners — from greeting the neighbors in a Yogyakarta boarding house to telling the story of last weekend, with ngoko and krama and clear rules for when to use each.

product.title: Javanese 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Javanese: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Javanese builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary with each word's krama form and an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. Javanese grammar is refreshingly simple — no verb endings, no tenses, no gender — so the one thing that is truly new is undha-usuk: the speech levels ngoko and krama, which decide which word you use with whom. This course teaches them in pairs from the very first unit instead of saving them for the end: every word comes with its krama form, every dialogue shows who is speaking to whom. Plus the pronunciation points rarely taught openly — the a that sounds like o, d/t versus dh/th, and the three kinds of e.

blocks.text: Javanese is spoken by some **eighty million people** — more than German, Korean or Italian. It is the most widely spoken regional language in the world. If you spend time in Indonesia, it is probably the language you will hear most after Indonesian itself: in the market, at the late-night street stall, in family group chats, in the songs the shuttle driver plays at three in the morning. And if you are not Javanese, it is probably also the language that most often leaves you standing on the other side of the fence.

This course is written to bring you inside that fence. Not so you can read the *Serat Centhini*, and not so you can memorize a hundred honorific words in a week. The goal is far simpler and far more useful: to let you open your mouth at a food stall, greet the neighbors, answer your landlady, and laugh along in conversations that used to pass you by.

Here is the good news before page one, and it is big news: **Javanese grammar is remarkably simple.** Verbs never change for the person — *aku mangan, kowé mangan, dhèwèké mangan* (I eat, you eat, she eats), one form for everyone. There are no tenses that change the verb; "already" and "going to" are marked with the little words *wis* and *arep*, and that's it. No grammatical gender, no cases, no articles. Word order is the same as in English: subject, verb, object.

Much of the vocabulary is also shared with Indonesian and Malay, which Javanese has lived next to for centuries: *omah* (house), *anak* (child), *mata* (eye), *tangan* (hand), *dalan* (road), *sapa* (who), *pira* (how much), *lunga* (go). If you already know some Indonesian, many basic words will feel like old friends with a slightly shifted sound; if you don't, nothing in this course assumes you do.
There are difficulties too, and this course names them now so they don't ambush you halfway. There are two, and only two.

**The first: undha-usuk, the speech levels.** Javanese has two levels used every day — **ngoko** for friends your age and people younger than you, **krama** for people you show respect to. It isn't just the tone that changes, it's **the words**. "Eat" is *mangan* in ngoko and *nedha* in krama; "house" is *omah* and *griya*; "go" is *lunga* and *késah*. To a beginner this feels like learning two languages at once, and that is why many people give up in week two.

This course handles it differently from most books: **krama is not piled up in the back chapters.** It comes in pairs from Unit 1. Every vocabulary table has a krama column; every dialogue shows who is talking to whom; and the good news that textbooks rarely mention is that **the words with a separate krama form are limited.** About eight hundred, and the truly frequent ones number fewer than two hundred. Thousands of other words are identical at both levels. You are not memorizing two languages. You are memorizing two hundred extra words.

**The second: pronunciation.** Javanese uses the Latin alphabet, but the letters don't always sound the way you'd guess. The letter **a** at the end of a word sounds like **o** — *apa* comes out as "opo", *sapa* as "sopo", *lara* as "loro". There are **two kinds of d and two kinds of t** (*dara* is not *dhara*, *tuku* is not *thuthuk*), and the difference really changes meaning. And there are **three kinds of e**. This is the part people most often skip, yet it is exactly what makes you sound Javanese rather than like someone reading aloud. A pronunciation chapter is waiting just ahead, and every vocabulary table has a "Say it" column.

The dialogues follow **Dian**, a university student from Jakarta who has just moved to Yogyakarta, her friend **Ahmad**, and the people around her: **Rini**, the neighbor in her boarding house, the same age and therefore addressed in ngoko; **Pak Broto**, the much older landlord, who must be addressed in krama; and **Mbak Sri**, who runs the food stall near the boarding house. Seen from both directions of these conversations, undha-usuk becomes something alive, not a table to memorize.

What they talk about is deliberately ordinary: finding a room, bargaining at the market, ordering rice, asking the way to Malioboro, a stomachache, market days, weekend plans. The language people really use is the language of ordinary things.

Twenty units, one story per unit, about twenty to thirty minutes a sitting. Do one unit every two days and in six weeks you will reach the last page with enough to open your mouth in Yogyakarta — and, more importantly, with ears good enough to understand the answer. *Sugeng sinau* — happy studying.

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place, and krama is built up little by little from Unit 1.

blocks.text: This course is designed for **self-study**. Each unit is meant to be finished in one sitting of about 20-30 minutes. What matters is not how fast you move forward, but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same layout, in a deliberate order:

items: **Dialogue** — first read the Javanese aloud without looking at the translation. Let your ears work before your brain demands explanations.

**Literal translation** — the small italic line under the translation. This is the part people skip most, yet it is where you see how Javanese *thinks*. Example: *Jenengku Dian* literally means "name-my Dian" — no word for "is", and the owner sticks to the end of the word.
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever felt strange.
**Vocabulary** — the new words of the unit, in **four columns**: the ngoko form, the krama form, how to say it, and the meaning.
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you have really tried.

blocks.title: Reading the krama column
items: If the **Krama** column shows a **–**, the word is **the same** in ngoko and krama. That's true of most Javanese words, and it's the good news: you only need to learn twice the words whose column is filled.

If the column is filled, learn the words **in pairs**, together, in one breath: *mangan – nedha*, *omah – griya*, *lunga – késah*. Learning them separately, ngoko first and krama later, is the most exhausting way to learn Javanese.

Some words have a third form, **krama inggil**, used to *honor the person being talked about* — for example *dhahar* for the "eating" of someone you respect. This A1 course mentions it when such a word is truly common, but doesn't ask you to use it. Plain krama already makes you polite.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: From Unit 3 on, each unit asks you to review an earlier one — usually two steps back, just far enough to make your memory work without feeling like starting over. The method is reversed: cover the Javanese, look at the English, and rebuild the Javanese sentences from memory.
This is what turns "I once understood it" into "I can use it". Don't skip it.

blocks.text: One last rule: **say it out loud**. Javanese is written in familiar Latin letters, and that is the trap — your eyes will read it like English, but it sounds different. The "Say it" column in every vocabulary table is not decoration; it is a core part of the lesson. Capital letters mark the stressed syllable: **AH-koo** (*aku*, I) means the stress falls on the *a*.

Read this chapter once now, then come back whenever a word seems to make no sense. No need to memorize it — ninety percent will stick by itself through the dialogues. But do read it once carefully, because this is where Javanese holds most of its surprises. The "Say it" column uses this key: **ah** as in *father* · **o** as in *law* or British *hot* (never "oh-oo") · **ee** as in *see* · **i** (before a consonant) as in *sit* · **oo** as in *food* · **uh** as in *about* · **ay** as in *say*, but pure, without the glide · **eh** as in *bed* · **ow** as in *how* · **ch** as in *church* · **ng** as in *singer*, also at the start of a word · **ny** as in *canyon* · **'** a catch in the throat, as in *uh-oh*. **dh** and **th** are special Javanese sounds (see below) — **th** is never the *th* of *think*. Capital letters mark the stress. Also: **c** is always *ch* as in *church*, **j** as in *jam*, **g** always hard as in *go*, and **r** is lightly rolled, as in Spanish or Scottish English.
Rule number one: the a that sounds like o

If you only have time to learn one thing from this chapter, learn this. **A letter *a* in an open syllable at the end of a word sounds like *o***, and if the syllable before it is also open and has an *a*, it changes too. It's not the *o* of "go" but a more open *o*, like the vowel in *law* or British *hot*.

**The rule is cancelled as soon as the word is closed or gets a suffix.** Compare: *apa* → "**opo**", but *apané* → "**ah-PAH-nay**". *Lara* → "**loro**", but *larané* → "**lah-RAH-nay**". Once a consonant or an extra syllable follows, the *a* goes back to *a*. Words whose last syllable is closed don't change in the first place: *pasar* (market) → **PAH-sahr**.

blocks.title: A quick way to remember it
items: Look at the last letter of the word. If the word **ends in the letter *a***, say *o*. If it ends in a consonant or another vowel, leave it alone.

If the final *a* turns into *o*, check the syllable before it: if it is also open with an *a*, it becomes *o* too (*sapa* → so-po; *bapak* → BAH-pahk does not, because *ba-* is closed off by the *p*).
Throughout this course the "Say it" column has already worked out the result for you. But once you read Javanese outside this course, this rule is what will save you.

blocks.text: Three kinds of e

English spells many vowel sounds with the letter *e* and leaves you to guess. Javanese has **three** *e* sounds, and its standard spelling tells them apart. This course uses that distinction consistently.

Name

Example
rows: the weak *uh* in *about* — no special mouth shape ("Say it": **uh**)
like *ay* in *say*, but pure, mouth slightly narrowed ("Say it": **ay**)
like *e* in *bed*, mouth more open ("Say it": **eh**)

blocks.text: The difference between *é* and *è* is small and rarely changes meaning, so don't worry if you mix them up — Javanese speakers themselves vary by region. What you **must** keep apart is the **pepet** (*e*) from the other two, because that difference is real: *sega* (rice) is not *séga*, and *tela* (cassava) is not *téla*.

blocks.title: When the accents are left out
items: Outside this course — on street signs, T-shirts, WhatsApp messages — Javanese speakers almost never write *é* and *è*. Everything is written as plain *e*.
So don't be confused if you see *kowe*, *dhewe*, *manehe*. They are the same words; the accents are simply dropped. This course uses them so you get the sounds right from the start.

blocks.text: Two kinds of d and two kinds of t

Here is a sound pair that really changes meaning. Javanese has **plain d/t** (tongue touching the back of the upper teeth, like Spanish or French *d/t*) and **dh/th** (tongue pulled back so the tip touches the roof of the mouth — a thicker, duller sound, like English *d* and *t* in "door" and "top", only further back). Despite the spelling, **th has nothing to do with English *th***.

head: Pair
First meaning
Second meaning
rows: female — the correct form is *wédok*, with a plain d

blocks.text: **How to practice:** say a plain dental *d*, then pull the tip of your tongue back about a centimeter from your teeth toward the roof of your mouth, and say it again. That second sound is *dh*. If it's still hard, an ordinary English *d* and *t* will do — they already sit a little further back than the Javanese plain *d/t*, and context will help you be understood nine times out of ten. But don't **swap them the other way**: a *dh* for a plain *d* sounds odder than the reverse.

blocks.text: Stress

Javanese stress is **weak and flat** — far flatter than English. It usually falls on the **second-to-last syllable**: **SO-po**, **O-mah**, **ngom-BAY**. If the second-to-last syllable has a pepet (*e*), the stress moves to the last syllable: *sega* → **suh-GO**, *tenan* → **tuh-NAHN**.

Don't spend time on this. Wrong stress in Javanese almost never makes you misunderstood. Throughout the course, capital letters in the "Say it" column mark it for you — use them as a guide, not as something to memorize. In fact, the biggest favor you can do yourself is to stress *less* than you would in English.

blocks.title: The chapter in one paragraph
items: *a* at the end of a word → **o**. This rule will save you most often.
There are three *e*'s: pepet (weak *uh*), *é* (*say*), *è* (*bed*). Only the pepet must be kept apart from the other two.
*dh* and *th* = tongue pulled back. If you can't yet, use English *d* and *t* and keep going.
Everything else is spelled the way it sounds, consistently. Javanese has no other surprises in store.

front.title: Undha-usuk: ngoko, krama, and when to use them

blocks.text: This chapter is a map. Read it once now so you see the overall shape, then come back whenever a unit makes you wonder "why is this a different word?". You don't need to memorize anything here — the twenty units ahead will put it in place bit by bit.
What actually changes

In English, politeness lives mostly in **forms of address** and **tone**: "Where you off to, mate?" versus "Where are you going, sir?". The basic verbs and nouns stay the same. Javanese handles it by **swapping the words themselves**.

Look at the first row: **not a single word is the same**. That's why Javanese feels like two languages to a beginner. But look too at how **the structure is identical** — subject, time marker, verb, question word, in exactly the same order. Only the vocabulary changes. The grammar is one.
When to use which

head: To whom
Level
Examples
rows: Friends your age, younger siblings, children, people you're close to
classmates, cousins your age, the neighbor in your boarding house
Older people, people you've just met, bosses, teachers, officials, in-laws
the landlord, lecturers, a much older market seller, your partner's parents
*kula* not *aku*, *nyuwun* not *njaluk* — lowering yourself, not raising the listener
The actions of someone you honor
*Bapak dhahar* (Father eats), not *Bapak nedha* — raising that person

blocks.title: Emergency rules for beginners
items: **When in doubt, use krama.** Krama to a friend your age sounds too formal and a bit funny, but it never offends. Ngoko to an older person can sound rude. Erring on the polite side costs far less.

**If your krama runs out, switch to Indonesian.** This is what people in Java really do every day, Javanese speakers included: they switch to Indonesian as soon as their krama isn't enough. Mixing *Bapak sampun dhahar?* (Have you eaten, sir?) with Indonesian is far better than forcing ngoko.

**People will forgive you.** Javanese speakers know perfectly well that undha-usuk is hard — Javanese children take over a decade to master it, and many young Javanese admit their krama is a mess. Simply trying earns you half the social credit.

blocks.text: How much there is to learn

A reassuring number: Javanese has about **eight hundred** words whose krama form differs from ngoko. That sounds like a lot until you compare it with the tens of thousands of other words that are **exactly the same at both levels**. And of those eight hundred, fewer than two hundred come up in everyday conversation — and those are what this course contains.

There are also **patterns** that lighten the load, so it isn't blind memorization. What changes **regularly** — learn it once and it applies everywhere — falls into two groups: the **suffixes and prefixes** attached to nouns and verbs, and a handful of **function words** that appear in almost every sentence.

The last five rows matter enormously and you'll use them in almost every sentence: **ora → boten**, **wis → sampun**, **arep → badhé**, **karo → kaliyan**, **menyang → dhateng**. These five words alone make your sentence sound krama even if the rest isn't perfect — and people really do this: slipping five krama function words into an otherwise simple sentence is the cheapest way to sound polite. Learn all five now; the rest will come through the dialogues.

blocks.title: What this course does not teach
items: **Madya** — a middle level between ngoko and krama, used in markets and in half-familiar conversation. It's real and often heard, but its rules aren't tidy enough to teach at A1. You'll absorb it yourself once your krama is solid.
**Full krama inggil** — this course mentions only the most common krama inggil words (*dhahar*, *tindak*, *saré*, *ngendika*, *pirsa*), as an introduction. Mastering it is A2-and-up work.
**Javanese script** — the beautiful letters ꦲꦤꦕꦫꦏ. This course uses the Latin alphabet throughout, because that's what Javanese speakers use every day to write their own language.

blocks.text: Numbers
Combining forms before *puluh* (ten), *atus* (hundred), *èwu* (thousand): **se-, rong, telung, patang, limang, nem, pitung, wolung, sangang**.
Pronunciation — three rules

items: **a at the end of a word sounds like o**, and an open syllable before it changes too: *apa* → **opo**, *sapa* → **sopo**. Cancelled as soon as the word is closed or gets a suffix: *apané* → **ah-PAH-nay**.
**Three kinds of e**: pepet (*sega* → SUH-go), closed taling (*kowé* → ko-WAY), open taling (*manèh* → MAH-neh). Only the pepet must be kept apart from the other two.
**dh and th**: tongue pulled back from the teeth toward the roof of the mouth — never the English *th*. *wedi* (afraid) is not *wedhi* (sand).
